title: Chapter 8: Tripura Culture — Tribes, Festivals, Art and Languages

blocks.content: Tripura has two broad communities — the indigenous tribal peoples (about 31% of population) and the Bengali settlers (about 69% of population). The tribal communities belong to 19 officially notified tribes, of which the Tripuri (Twipra) is the largest. Bengali Hindus are the demographic majority, with a significant Muslim population (mostly of Bengali origin).

blocks.content: Kokborok (also written as Kok Borok) is the language of the Tripuri (Twipra) people — the original tribal inhabitants of Tripura. It is a Tibeto-Burman language belonging to the Bodo-Garo branch. Kokborok is one of the two official languages of Tripura (along with Bengali). It is spoken by approximately 16-20% of Tripura's population.

items: Official language: Kokborok has been one of Tripura's official languages since 1979
Script: The traditional Koloma script is used; also written in Roman and Bengali scripts
Literature: Ancient literature in Rajmala (royal chronicle); modern literature is growing
Government promotion: Radio, TV programmes in Kokborok; textbooks published
Kokborok Sahitya Sabha: The apex literary organisation for Kokborok language
Issue: The script controversy — some prefer the Roman script while others use Bengali or Koloma; politically sensitive

blocks.content: NOTE: Kharchi Puja is the most spectacular festival of Tripura. The name comes from 'khar' (sin) and 'chi' (cleansing) — a festival to cleanse sin from the land. The 14 deities worshipped are collectively called Chaturdasha Devata and are the royal deities of the Manikya dynasty. The festival at Old Agartala temple draws 5-6 lakh visitors over 7 days, making it one of northeast India's largest religious gatherings.

The Hojagiri dance of the Reang (Bru) tribe of Tripura has been recognised as a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Performed by young women of the Reang tribe on the occasion of Kojagiri Lakshmi Puja (full moon of Ashwin), the dance is celebrated for its extraordinary grace and balance.

items: Performers: Young women (3-10 dancers typically); girls as young as 8 years old perform
Props: Dancers balance earthen pitchers on their heads while standing on earthen pots; hold lighted oil lamps, fans, and bottles; all while dancing
Music: Accompanied by kham (drum), sumui (flute), and chongpreng (string instrument)
Significance: Worship of Lakshmi; prayer for prosperity; the balancing represents stability and grace
UNESCO recognition: Included in UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2023
This is Tripura's greatest cultural achievement in global recognition

blocks.content: Neermahal (meaning 'Water Palace') in Rudrasagar Lake, Udaipur (South Tripura), is the only floating palace in northeast India. Built in the middle of Rudrasagar Lake, it was constructed in 1930 by Maharaja Bir Bikram Kishore Manikya Bahadur as a summer palace. The architecture combines Mughal and Hindu styles — a unique fusion.

items: Area: Covers about 83,000 sq ft; accessed only by boat
Rooms: 24 rooms and a large hall; 2-storey structure
Architecture: Mughal arches combined with Hindu temple-style turrets and mandapas
Tourist attractions: Annual Neermahal Tourism Festival; boat races on Rudrasagar Lake; spectacular night illumination
Conservation: Under Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) for restoration and conservation
